place.zh: 体育馆 · 院系杯决赛 · 十二月十九日
place.en: The gym · the cup final · 19 December

setup.zh: 三趟厕所，葛奶奶在看台最高一排织袜子，第一百天，爸「就位」。零点六秒，落后一分，大刘伤了，换上来的人罚两个。他翻过那只「0」号纸杯站了起来，走了十几步。头一个，砸在前沿上。还剩一个。
setup.en: Three trips to the toilet; Granny Ge knitting in the top row; day one hundred; his dad "in position." Point six of a second, a point down, Big Liu hurt: whoever comes on shoots two. He turns over the cup marked "0", stands, and walks a dozen-odd steps. The first hits the front of the rim. One left.

recap.zh: 决赛最后一罚，他是哆嗦着投的——怕是带着走的，进了。
recap.en: The last free throw of the final he shot shaking: fear is carried, not crushed, and it went in.

zh: 最末那只纸杯，翻过来了。
en: Point six of a second, one point down.
The last paper cup, turned over.

story.zh:
十二月十九日，晚上六点五十二分，新地板的漆味还没散尽。看台坐满了，过道里也站满了，站着的比坐着的多。替补席上，阿禾摆好一排纸杯，十二只，杯口朝下，最末那一只写着「0」，自打十一月他崴了脚，就再没翻过来。

他已经去了三趟厕所。第三趟出门的时候，阿禾头也没抬：「第三趟了。」他不知道她连这个也数。

第三趟回来，他在看台上找人。看台最高一排，葛奶奶戴着蓝布套袖在织袜子，老花镜挂在链子上；她跟邻座说，她不看球，来看看「那个天天来抄书的孩子，到底是干什么的」。老蔡在第一排举着那块硬纸板：「沈道友稳」。眼镜坐在他旁边，脸朝着另一边，真的像不认识他。沈芒冲他们笑了一下，笑得像牙疼。

六点五十五，阿禾把首发的五个名字念了一遍，又把替补的七个念了一遍，念到最后一个，「沈芒」，她没有停，也没有快，跟念别人一样。然后她往后翻新的一页，翻过十月里一页，他眼尖，看见一行：「沈芒　为什么打球　答：想跑快一点　信一半」。耳朵还没烧完，她已经写下：「12月19日　9/11 起，今天第一百天。」

「一百天怎么了？」

「头两个月长的是神经，手学会了；三个月上下，长的才是身子本身。」她把笔帽按上，「九月十一号，你吐在跑道边上。」

家长群里，他爸发来一张照片：家里那台旧电视放着直播，他爸一条腿架在小板凳上，膝盖缠着护膝，旁边一盘瓜子。底下两个字：「就位。」

七点跳球。中药学院穿着马氏大药房新送的金字球衣，马小宝在篮下像一堵墙，谁来都撞回去。开场第三个回合，大刘在篮下起跳，马小宝跟着起跳，比他高出半个头，一巴掌把球扇到了看台上，扇进了第三排一个女生的爆米花桶里，爆米花飞起来一片。中药那边的看台「嗷」地一声。第一节打完，中药领先九分。

第二节，针推的队长一个人连投带突，追回两分。他话少，打球也话少，不庆祝，不吼，进了球就往回跑，跑过替补席的时候，拿手背在纸杯那一排上蹭一下，像在数数。蹭到最末那一只，手背停了一停，过去了。半场打完，针推落后七分。

第三节，一个球滚出底线，停在沈芒脚边。他弯腰捡起来要递过去——看台上几百双眼睛顺着那个球，一齐落到了他身上。他的手一抖，球滑了出去，弹到裁判的脚面上。

看台上「哄」地笑开了：「零号！上场概率涨到百分之二了！」

他坐回板凳，脸一直红到耳朵根。沈芒啊沈芒，球都递不出去，还罚球。场边阿禾低头写了一行；那一行写的什么，他不敢想。

他坐在板凳上。嘴是干的，喝了水也是干的；手心凉，凉里头还冒汗；他坐着不动，都能觉出脖子上那根血管一下一下地跳；场上的声音一阵一阵远了，像有人在慢慢拧小收音机。台子上那一串小结，这会儿全在他身上，一节一节，都醒着。

第四节，大刘又上去了，四次犯规，一次也不敢再犯，只好拿身子挡，挡一回，被马小宝撞退一步。比分一分一分咬回来。最后两分钟，针推一个三分追平了；马小宝在篮下转身打板，挨了一下，加罚也进，又领先三分；大刘咬着牙勾手，拉回到只差一分。看台上的人全站起来了，坐着的只剩葛奶奶，袜子织到了脚后跟。最后十秒，六十一比六十二。大刘转身往篮下冲，马小宝横着跨过来，两个人在半空撞在一处。哨响。大刘落地，左脚正踩在马小宝的鞋上，脚脖子往外一拐，抱着脚坐在了地上。马小宝愣了一愣，先蹲了下去，伸手去扶他的脚脖子，嘴里道：「没事吧？没事吧？」——那语气，倒不像对手。

马小宝犯规，罚球两次。比赛时间：零点六秒。

大刘站不起来了。

「受伤的不能罚。」雷老师在记录台后头站起来，「换上来的人罚。」

看台上嗡的一声。第一排的眼镜扶了扶眼镜，对老蔡道：「我查了。受伤队员的罚球，由替他上场的那个人来罚。规则上写着的。」老蔡道：「那谁上？」眼镜没答，往替补席的最末一个座位看了一眼。

大刘被架过替补席，经过最末那个座位，喘着粗气，只说了两个字：「零号。」

沈芒没动。

他脑子里一下子排出来一串理由，一条比一条体面：手凉；没热身；九号投篮比他多练了三年；凑数的，本来就不该上。冒到最后一条，竟是他爸的腔调，九月里视频那头那一句：跑不过，就走。

他的屁股，在板凳上，像是生了根。

他抬起头，看见那一排纸杯。十一只都翻过来了，杯底湿着。最末那一只还扣着，那个「0」字黑黑的，朝着他。

他伸手把它翻了过来，空着喝了一口，放下。然后站了起来。腿是软的，他照样站起来了。

从替补席到罚球线，十几步。这十几步里，体育馆像是一下子变大了。灯太亮，看台太高，四面八方全是手机，一个一个亮着，像一片一片的眼睛。罚球线两边站好了人，马小宝站在最靠篮下的位置，两手撑着膝盖，冲他歪了歪头。他往场边看了一眼：阿禾没看他，低着头，笔尖停在纸上，像在等。

中药那边的看台有人喊起来，跟着十几个人一齐喊，有了节拍：「百分之一！百分之一！」他想起十六号那天，十一个人围着他喊。这回是几百个。马小宝站在篮下，冲他点点头，声音不高：「慢慢来，零号。不着急。」

裁判把球递给他。规则上，拿到球五秒之内得出手。他脑子里只剩一个念头：快，快，扔出去，扔出去就不用站在这儿了。球在手里，比他投过的两千多个都沉，皮面上的颗粒一粒一粒硌着汗湿的手心。他拍都没拍，屈膝，抬手——

「当」，砸在篮筐前沿上，弹了出来。

看台上一半人叹气，一半人叫好。中药那边的替补席跳了起来。他耳朵里「嗡」的一声，什么也听不见了，只看见马小宝的嘴在动。

还剩一个。
story.en:
December 19th, 6:52 p.m., and the smell of varnish on the new floor hadn't cleared yet. The stands were full, the aisles were full, more standing than sitting. On the bench, Ahe set out a row of paper cups, twelve of them, mouths down; the last one had "0" on it and hadn't been turned over since he twisted his ankle in November.

He had already been to the toilet three times. As he went out the third time, Ahe didn't look up: "That's three." He hadn't known she counted that too.

Back from the third trip, he searched the stands. In the top row Granny Ge was knitting socks in her blue cloth oversleeves, her reading glasses hanging on their chain; she was telling her neighbor she wasn't here for the game, she'd come to see "what that boy who copies books every day actually does." In the front row Old Cai held up the piece of cardboard: "Steady, Daoist Friend Shen." Specs sat beside him with his face turned the other way, really as if he didn't know him. Shen Mang gave them a smile that looked like toothache.

At 6:55 Ahe read out the five starters, then the seven substitutes, and when she reached the last name, "Shen Mang," she neither paused nor hurried — the same as everyone else. Then she flipped to a new page further back, past a page from October, and his sharp eyes caught a line: "Shen Mang  why he plays  answer: wants to run a bit faster  half believed". Before his ears had finished burning, she had already written: "Dec 19  from 9/11, today is day one hundred."

"What about a hundred days?"

"For the first two months, what grows is the nerves — the hands learn. At around three months, that's when the body itself grows." She clicked the cap back on her pen. "September 11th, you threw up beside the track."

In the parents' group, his dad sent a photo: the old TV at home showing the livestream, his dad with one leg propped on a little stool, a brace wrapped around the knee, a plate of sunflower seeds beside him. Below it, two words: "In position."

Tip-off at seven. The College of Chinese Materia Medica wore new gold-lettered jerseys donated by Ma's Pharmacy, and Ma Xiaobao was a wall under the basket; whoever came in got bounced off it. In the third possession Big Liu went up under the basket and Ma Xiaobao went up with him, half a head taller, and swatted the ball into the stands — into a girl's popcorn bucket in the third row, popcorn flying everywhere. The Materia Medica stands roared. End of the first quarter, Materia Medica by nine.

In the second, the Acupuncture and Tuina captain clawed back two on his own, shooting and driving. He said little, played quiet, didn't celebrate, didn't shout; he scored and ran back, and as he passed the bench he brushed the back of his hand along the row of paper cups, as if counting. At the last cup the hand paused a moment, then moved on. At the half, Acupuncture and Tuina were down seven.

In the third quarter, a ball rolled out over the baseline and stopped at Shen Mang's feet. He bent to pick it up and hand it over — and hundreds of eyes in the stands followed the ball and landed, all at once, on him. His hand shook; the ball slipped out and bounced off the referee's foot.

The stands burst out laughing: "Number Zero! Chance of playing just went up to two percent!"

He sat back down, red to the ears. Shen Mang, oh Shen Mang — you can't even hand over a ball, and you'd shoot free throws. On the sideline Ahe bent her head and wrote a line; what it said, he didn't dare think.

He sat on the bench. His mouth was dry, and stayed dry after a drink of water; his palms were cold, and sweating inside the cold; sitting still, he could feel the vessel in his neck thumping; the noise on the court faded away in waves, as if someone were slowly turning down a radio. That chain of little knots from the table was all inside him now, every one of them awake.

In the fourth quarter Big Liu went back on with four fouls, not daring another, able only to block with his body — and each time, Ma Xiaobao knocked him back a step. The score came back point by point. In the last two minutes a three from Acupuncture and Tuina tied it; Ma Xiaobao spun under the basket and banked it in through contact, made the free throw, up by three again; Big Liu gritted his teeth and hooked one in, back to one point down. The whole gym was on its feet, all but Granny Ge, whose sock had reached the heel. Ten seconds left, sixty-one to sixty-two. Big Liu spun and drove for the basket; Ma Xiaobao stepped across, and the two of them collided in midair. Whistle. Big Liu landed with his left foot right on Ma Xiaobao's shoe, his ankle turned out, and he sat down on the floor clutching his foot. Ma Xiaobao froze for an instant, then crouched down first, reaching for the ankle: "You all right? You all right?" — not the voice of an opponent.

Foul on Ma Xiaobao, two free throws. Time on the clock: zero point six seconds.

Big Liu couldn't get up.

"The injured player can't shoot," said Coach Lei, standing up behind the scorer's table. "The sub shoots."

A murmur ran through the stands. In the front row Specs pushed up his glasses and said to Old Cai, "I checked. An injured player's free throws are taken by whoever comes on for him. It's in the rules." Old Cai said, "So who comes on?" Specs didn't answer; he glanced at the last seat on the bench.

Big Liu was helped off past the bench, and as he passed the last seat, breathing hard, he said only two words: "Number Zero."

Shen Mang didn't move.

A string of reasons lined up in his head at once, each more respectable than the last: cold hands; no warm-up; Number Nine had three more years of shooting than he did; a number-filler, who shouldn't be out there in the first place. The last one to surface came in his dad's voice, that line from the video call in September: if you can't outrun it, walk away.

His backside seemed to have taken root on the bench.

He looked up and saw the row of paper cups. All eleven had been turned over, their bottoms wet. The last one was still mouth down, the "0" on it black, facing him.

He reached out and turned it over, took a sip from the empty cup, and set it down. Then he stood up. His legs were weak; he stood up anyway.

From the bench to the free-throw line, a dozen-odd steps. In those steps the gym seemed to swell. The lights too bright, the stands too high, phones on every side, lit one by one, like fields of eyes. Players lined up on either side of the lane; Ma Xiaobao stood in the spot nearest the basket, hands on his knees, and tilted his head at him. He glanced at the sideline: Ahe wasn't looking at him; head down, pen point resting on the page, as if waiting.

Someone in the Materia Medica stands started shouting, then a dozen more joined in, and it found a beat: "One percent! One percent!" He thought of the 16th, eleven people yelling around him. This was hundreds. Ma Xiaobao stood under the basket and nodded at him, his voice low: "Take your time, Number Zero. No hurry."

The referee handed him the ball. By the rules, you have five seconds from the ball to the shot. One thought was left in his head: quick, quick, get rid of it, get rid of it and you won't have to stand here. The ball in his hands was heavier than any of the two thousand-odd he'd shot, the grain of the leather pressing into his sweat-soaked palms. He didn't even bounce it; he bent his knees, raised his hands—

Clang. It hit the front of the rim and bounced out.

Half the stands groaned, half cheered. The Materia Medica bench leapt up. His ears went "whoomp" and he heard nothing at all; he only saw Ma Xiaobao's mouth moving.

One left.

label.en: In four, out six, shoot shaking

exits.means: breathes in four, out six, and shoots the last free throw shaking

refuse.zh: 手还在抖。裁判把球递了回来。
refuse.en: His hands still shake. The referee hands back the ball.

story.zh:
裁判把球收回去，等两边站好。这几秒钟，是规则留给他的。

他不想了，换了一样做：吸四拍，吐六拍，吐得慢得像要把肚子里的东西全倒干净。阿禾十月里说过，这是踩刹车；十六号夜里他在手环上自己看见了——刹得住一截，刹不干净。手还在抖。可这个动作他在北风里做了两千多回，熟到用不着想；熟了的事，交给身子去做，抖着也做得出来。

耳朵里那层嗡嗡的东西退下去一点，他听见一个声音，很小，很近：场边，阿禾那支笔，「嗒」地按了一下。

她要记了。不管进不进，她都要记。

怕还在那儿，看台上的人一个也没少。可怕，原来不是压下去的，是带着走的。

他拍了两下球，屈膝，抬手。手是哆嗦的，他没等它不哆嗦。

球砸在篮筐后沿，弹起来，落回筐上，沿着铁圈转了一圈，又转了半圈。看台上那声「百分之一」，喊到一半，停了。

它掉了进去。

他还举着手，嘴里冒出两个字，小得只有自己听得见：「成了！」
story.en:
The referee took the ball back and waited for both sides to set. These few seconds were what the rules left him.

He stopped thinking, and did something else instead: in for four counts, out for six, breathing out so slowly it was as if he were emptying out everything inside him. Ahe had said in October that this was stepping on the brake; on the night of the 16th he'd seen it for himself on the band — it brakes part of it, not all of it. His hands were still shaking. But he had done this two thousand-odd times in the north wind, so often he didn't need to think about it; and what you've done that often, you can hand over to the body, and it can do it even while shaking.

The droning layer in his ears receded a little, and he heard a sound, very small, very close: at the sideline, Ahe's pen went click.

She was going to write it down. In or not, she was going to write it down.

The fear was still there, and not one person in the stands had left. But fear, it turned out, wasn't something you pressed down. It was something you carried with you.

He bounced the ball twice, bent his knees, raised his hands. His hands were trembling; he didn't wait for them to stop.

The ball hit the back of the rim, bounced up, dropped back onto it, rolled once around the iron hoop, then half again. The "One percent" from the stands stopped halfway.

It dropped in.

His hands still raised, two words slipped out of him, so quiet only he could hear: "Done it!"
